analysis.one_liner: Requires large electric and gas utilities to deliver escalating cuts in customer energy use through 2035.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and its Energy Subcommittee the day after introduction, never received a vote or any further action, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first national energy efficiency resource standard. Large electric utilities and large natural gas distribution companies would have had to achieve growing cumulative savings in the energy their customers use — reaching 27% cumulative electricity savings and 20% cumulative gas savings by 2035 — through efficiency upgrades, weatherization, better building codes, appliance standards, and reduced system losses [S2] [S3]. Companies that fell short would owe federal civil penalties, and states could run their own equivalent or tougher programs instead [S3]. The bill sat in committee from the day it was introduced and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses would benefit through lower energy bills: the bill requires savings to come from measures that are cost-effective by a defined societal benefit-cost test, and counts weatherization, heating and cooling repairs, insulation, air sealing, and efficient appliances — upgrades that particularly help people in older, drafty homes [S3]. Third-party efficiency providers and energy service companies would gain a large new market for delivering verified savings [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets mandatory, escalating savings targets for large utilities — 27% cumulative electricity savings and 20% cumulative gas savings by 2035 — rather than leaving efficiency to voluntary utility programs [S3].

Counts weatherization, insulation, window and door replacement, air sealing, and heating-and-cooling upgrades toward the targets, measures that cut bills most for people in poorly insulated housing [S3].
Defines programs as cost-effective only if lifetime benefits exceed lifetime costs using a societal benefit-cost test, so savings must outweigh what customers pay for the programs [S3].
Lets states run their own stronger programs in lieu of the federal one, preserving existing state efficiency efforts, and lets state regulators keep authority over stricter local rules [S3].
Redirects federal penalty payments to states to fund cost-effective efficiency programs, so money from companies that miss their targets still gets spent on savings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large retail electricity suppliers (those delivering at least 1,000,000 megawatt-hours a year) and large natural gas distribution companies would bear compliance costs, reporting duties, and civil penalties of $100 per megawatt-hour or $10 per million Btu of missed savings [S3]. Those program costs would generally be recovered through customer rates, and the bill's 'sense of Congress' section encourages states to let utilities recover lost margins from lower sales and even earn shareholder incentives [S3]. Gas utilities would face shrinking sales as gas use is cut 20% cumulatively [S3].

drawbacks.text: Program costs are typically recovered through utility rates, so some of the bill's benefit to households would be offset by charges on bills; the bill's sense-of-Congress section encourages states to let utilities recover lost margins from reduced sales and earn shareholder incentives, which adds to ratepayer costs [S3].

Companies would have routes around the targets: they could buy verified savings from other suppliers or third parties in the same state (or same power pool with regulator approval), and states could allow 'alternative compliance payments' starting at $50 per megawatt-hour or $5 per million Btu, letting suppliers pay rather than achieve savings [S3].

The savings percentages are cumulative targets from a 3-year baseline, so early-year requirements are modest (1% electricity, 0.5% gas in 2021), and the Secretary could grant suppliers a delay of up to 2 years for the first reporting period, softening near-term impact [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanism — requiring utilities to fund efficiency that is cheaper than producing or delivering more energy — is generally one of the least expensive ways to lower energy bills and cut fuel use, and the bill's cost-effectiveness test is meant to keep program costs below the value of the savings [S3]. The real weaknesses are the escape valves: purchased savings, alternative compliance payments, and encouraged recovery of lost utility margins all mean customers could pay partly for targets that are missed or met on paper [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill went from introduction straight to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy Subcommittee, got no markup, vote, or floor action, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the American Energy Efficiency Act on November 4, 2021, joined by Rep. Yvette Clarke of New York; it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
The next day, November 5, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, never reached the House floor, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
Only two members sponsored the bill, and no committee or floor vote ever tested support for it [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large electric and gas utilities are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory efficiency obligations, civil penalties for missed targets, and a standard that would have cumulatively cut electricity sales 27% and gas sales 20% by 2035. Households got neither the lower bills nor the efficiency upgrades the bill was designed to produce.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish a federal energy efficiency resource standard for large electricity and gas suppliers.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it stayed in the Energy Subcommittee for the entire Congress.

against.name: Large electric and natural gas utilities
against.role: Suppliers subject to the proposed savings mandates and penalties
against.what_they_did: Would have faced compliance obligations cutting cumulative electricity sales 27% and gas sales 20% by 2035; the record contains no public expression of their position on this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no measure of party-line or bipartisan support either way.

industries.note: Suppliers delivering at least 1,000,000 megawatt-hours a year would have had to achieve cumulative savings reaching 27% of their baseline deliveries by 2035, face $100-per-megawatt-hour penalties for shortfalls, and see sales decline as customers use less. The bill does encourage states to let them recover program costs, lost margins, and shareholder incentives through rates, so much of the burden would land on customer bills.

Large local gas distribution companies would have had to cut cumulative gas use 20% by 2035, directly shrinking the product they sell, with $10-per-million-Btu penalties for missed savings. Their business depends on selling more gas, which runs against the bill's goal of cutting customers' gas bills and consumption.

industries.industry: Energy service companies and third-party efficiency providers
industries.note: The bill explicitly lets utilities count savings delivered by retailers, building owners, energy service companies, and financial institutions, and allows suppliers to buy verified savings from them — creating a large new market for efficiency work that also lowers customers' bills.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel power plants and gas producers
industries.note: A 27% cumulative cut in electricity use and 20% cut in gas consumption would have reduced demand for fuel burned for power and heating. Some fuel-switching savings are countable, so the bill does not uniformly exclude fossil energy, but the overall demand reduction works against fuel sellers.
